subject: Impact of processes on run speed?

messages.author: d4880d80370a2c2a
messages.subject: Impact of processes on run speed?
parts:
Could someone point me to resources or share insights on the estimated influence of the following topics on speed? 

Specific info/resource request topics:
1. Impact of number of posterior samples saved on speed (ignoring the compilation times). That is, would removing any or all monitors even make a major dent in speed?
2. Impact of performing various calculations for derived qtys on speed 


Vague background:
We are building an integrated population to estimate bird abundance across a gridded surface. Our model is severely slowed by the following:
1. Spacetime generalized additive model (for latent abundance) 
2. Jointly sampling the GAM coefficients (using AF_slice;  RW_block has inferior mixing speed). 
3. Calculations are vectorized  
4. No unnecessary calculations

I also read the Turek et al 2021 paper and I think we've done everything relevant in our model to implement their recommendations.   

Can provide more detail if necessary via dm

TIA, 

Jessica Burnett

messages.author: dd632bd3bbcdd7e9
messages.subject: Re: Impact of processes on run speed?
parts:
Hi Jessica,

I'll take a try at this, but as you recognize these can be nebulous topics!  See below.

On Wed, May 11, 2022 at 8:05 AM Jessica Burnett <jessicale...@gmail.com> wrote:
Could someone point me to resources or share insights on the estimated influence of the following topics on speed? 

Specific info/resource request topics:
1. Impact of number of posterior samples saved on speed (ignoring the compilation times). That is, would removing any or all monitors even make a major dent in speed?

Conceivably.  Sometimes people don't realize how quickly they can fill up tons of memory even on modern machines.  In case it helps, the calculation to do is:
number of monitored dimensions * number of iterations * 8 bytes per double precision number / 2^20 = # of gigabytes your posterior will fill.

If that is really large, it can impact processing speed as the computer spends time during the run with large memory management duties and accesses.

You can use the monitors2, which has its own thinning, thin2, as a way to save fewer samples of some nodes.  Often this is helpful for example for large numbers of latent states  or random effects.
2. Impact of performing various calculations for derived qtys on speed

It depends on what the calculations are, but potentially yes.  One thing I would try to avoid if you are in a performance crunch is stochastic predictive nodes.  In some cases, it can work well to get derived quantities after running the MCMC, but the exception is if the derived quantities are functions of many dimensions that return few dimensions, and you don't want to store the many dimensions in order to calculate these later.

Derived quantities may be calculated on every MCMC iteration even if they are only needed to be stored as output on thinning intervals.  It is on the development to-do list to provide a system that would save the unnecessary computation that may be occurring.

Vague background:
We are building an integrated population to estimate bird abundance across a gridded surface. Our model is severely slowed by the following:
1. Spacetime generalized additive model (for latent abundance) 
2. Jointly sampling the GAM coefficients (using AF_slice;  RW_block has inferior mixing speed).

Some ideas for you: RW_block using control parameter "tries = n" where n is a number such as half the number of dimensions.  This will run n repeats of the RW_block sampler, which can work well because each repeat is fast (compared to other methods) but if there is only one try and that is a rejection, then no mixing occurs on that iteration.  (Until recenly the tries argument did not appear in help(samplers), an oversight we fixed.)  AF_slice is indeed costly but can mix well.  It can also work well to break down the full set of GAM coefficients into smaller blocks and sample each smaller block using either RW_block or AF_slice.
 
3. Calculations are vectorized  

This helps when all the calculations will always be done together anyway in the structure of the model.  But it hurts if only individual elements would need to be calculated during an MCMC update of a parent parameter.

4. No unnecessary calculations

I also read the Turek et al 2021 paper and I think we've done everything relevant in our model to implement their recommendations.

Fantastic.  This sounds like a really challenging problem you're tackling.  Thanks for the posting.

-Perry

Can provide more detail if necessary via dm

TIA, 

Jessica Burnett
